chapter: Harlem, Redman's band and the Savoy
title: Russell Pop Smith: the trumpeter who could not read words
summary: Russell Smith, from Ripley, Ohio, could not read or write yet was a great first trumpeter and a sergeant in the First World War orchestra.

story.theme_name: Remembering the early trumpeters and their styles
story.community_name: Trumpeters I admired: rating the horn players

blocks.x: I want to ask you about you from Ohio and those Smith fellows, Russell and Joseph.
Russell and Joseph.
They were from Ohio, too, weren't they?
From Ripley, Ohio.
Ripley, Ohio. Tell me something about them.
That's right.
What kind of guys -- Russell Smith played in Cab Calloway's band when I was in there. I had some very great experiences with Russell. You know Russell couldn't read words.
Well, I know that, I know that.
But here was a man who was a first trumpet player, which is almost impossible that he couldn't read writing.
I know that.
He hadn't had any schooling.
That's right.
I remember writing his letters to his wife.
I know you did. I remember.
He would put the check in and have the money order made out and he would have to write. And here was a man that could play any kind of music that you put up before him.
Fantastic.
A first trumpet player, which shows you what a tremendous [ ] . He was a great -- in the First World War he was in the orchestra.
He went to Europe with Jim Brymn Brown -- Tim Brymn Brown. It was a New York orchestra. I forget the regiment.
This is Russell Smith we're talking about?
Yeah, that's right.
Right.
Russell Pop Smith.
Uh-huh.
And he joined the Army like today and tomorrow, from his trumpet playing, he became a sergeant.
Wow.
That's right, one day. And he could play any kind of trumpet. He could double tongue, triple tongue and play the most beautiful melody.
He sure did.
And he had range, and it was so funny the way -- his trumpet playing was so phenomenal that what I
remember about him, so you could be sitting in front of him in the band and you think he wasn't playing loud, but if you go out in front of the band, he'd be carrying over the whole trumpet section.
Yeah, piercing right straight out.
That's right, just right straight ahead.
A handsome, good-looking man, lithe and tall.
That's right, he was a very handsome man.
